title: Phil Ruffin marries Oleksandra Nikolayenko at Mar-a-Lago; Trump is best man
description_medium: Casino owner Phil Ruffin married Oleksandra Nikolayenko at Mar-a-Lago in 2008, with Donald Trump as his best man. Ruffin said Trump gave the couple their wedding guests’ accommodations. The two had met through a proposed Trump-branded hotel at Ruffin’s Treasure Island casino; that deal failed, but they later partnered on Trump International Hotel Las Vegas.
description_long: Phil Ruffin married Oleksandra Nikolayenko at Mar-a-Lago in 2008, with Donald Trump serving as best man. Ruffin said Trump gave the wedding guests their accommodations as a present, while the couple hired entertainer Lionel Richie. Nikolayenko had been Miss Ukraine in 2004. Ruffin and Trump’s friendship had grown out of real-estate discussions: Ruffin first considered adding a Trump-branded hotel to Treasure Island, his Las Vegas casino, but that deal did not proceed. They stayed in touch, and Trump later agreed to develop a hotel on a parcel Ruffin showed him. Trump International Hotel Las Vegas opened in 2008, the year of Ruffin’s wedding. The ceremony took place at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach. The personal celebration therefore sat alongside a business relationship between the two men, whose hotel project was opening as the recession began. AP later described Ruffin and Trump as both business partners and social friends.

corrected_wording.proposed: Phil Ruffin marries Oleksandra Nikolayenko at Mar-a-Lago; Trump is best man
corrected_wording.reason: AP identifies Ruffin as the correct spelling, confirms the 2008 wedding at Mar-a-Lago and Trump’s best-man role, and supplies related business context; it does not support the original personal allegation.

source_access_notes: Read the Associated Press profile, which reports the wedding, Trump’s role and gift, and the men’s earlier and later hotel dealings.
rationale: AP identifies Ruffin as the correct spelling, confirms the 2008 wedding at Mar-a-Lago and Trump’s best-man role, and supplies related business context; it does not support the original personal allegation.

title: St. Louis Tea Party protest draws more than 1,000 people in February 2009
description_medium: On February 27, 2009, more than 1,000 people gathered in St. Louis for a Tea Party protest against the federal recovery bill and the Obama administration. The event grew well beyond organizers’ expected turnout. Americans for Prosperity was among the groups that helped mobilize Tea Party activity.
description_long: A Tea Party protest in St. Louis drew more than 1,000 people on February 27, 2009, far above organizers’ initial expectation of 50 to 100. The demonstration opposed the $787 billion economic recovery bill and reflected early public mobilization against federal spending and the Obama administration. Contemporary coverage described similar protests in other cities that day. Americans for Prosperity, a conservative advocacy group founded by David Koch, was active in organizing Tea Party events and later became a major part of the movement’s infrastructure. Investigative reporting traced Koch-linked funding to Americans for Prosperity and described its support for Tea Party organizing. The scale of the Tea Party movement grew in the following years, with AFP playing a role in its organizing network.

corrected_wording.proposed: St. Louis Tea Party protest draws more than 1,000 people in February 2009
corrected_wording.reason: The local protest date and turnout are corroborated, while New Yorker reporting supports an AFP funding and organizing context; the evidence does not substantiate the original direct-funding and party-takeover claims.

source_access_notes: Read the St. Louis reporting in the Christian Science Monitor and the New Yorker’s investigation of Koch-linked support for Americans for Prosperity and Tea Party organizing.
blockers: The sources establish Koch-linked funding for Americans for Prosperity and the group’s Tea Party activity, but do not document direct Koch funding or direction of the February 27 St. Louis protest.
rationale: The local protest date and turnout are corroborated, while New Yorker reporting supports an AFP funding and organizing context; the evidence does not substantiate the original direct-funding and party-takeover claims.

title: Benjamin Netanyahu returns as Israel’s prime minister on March 31, 2009
description_medium: Israel’s Knesset approved Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government on March 31, 2009, with 69 votes in favor and 45 against; five members abstained. It was Netanyahu’s second premiership, following his 1996–1999 term. Years earlier, Netanyahu had stayed at the home of Charles Kushner, Jared Kushner’s father, establishing a longstanding family connection relevant to Jared’s later role in Donald Trump’s administration.
description_long: Benjamin Netanyahu returned to Israel’s premiership on March 31, 2009, after the Knesset approved his coalition government by 69 votes to 45, with five abstentions. It was Israel’s 32nd government and Netanyahu’s second term as prime minister; his first had run from 1996 to 1999. His coalition joined Likud with Yisrael Beiteinu, Shas, Labor and other parties. Netanyahu told parliament that he would seek peace with the Palestinians while the new government included a strong right-wing bloc. The formation followed Israel’s February 2009 election and 49 days of coalition negotiations. A later report on Jared Kushner’s ties to Israel recounted that Netanyahu had been a friend of the Kushner family and once stayed in the childhood home of Jared, who later became a senior adviser to Donald Trump. The 2009 event was Netanyahu’s return to office; the family friendship provides context for the later Trump administration relationship.

corrected_wording.proposed: Benjamin Netanyahu returns as Israel’s prime minister on March 31, 2009
corrected_wording.reason: The Israeli government record establishes the date and vote; contemporaneous reporting supplies coalition context, and later reporting documents the Netanyahu–Kushner family friendship.

source_access_notes: Read the Israeli government’s record of the 32nd government and contemporaneous coverage of its Knesset vote; read the Jerusalem Post profile for the Kushner-family connection.
rationale: The Israeli government record establishes the date and vote; contemporaneous reporting supplies coalition context, and later reporting documents the Netanyahu–Kushner family friendship.

title: TrumpFile publishes a broad overview of 2010s economic and political trends
description_medium: The 2010s overview links mall closures after the financial crisis, Fox News coverage of Barack Obama and Midwestern economic conditions, Missouri’s presidential votes in 2008 and 2012, and Russian investment in U.S. businesses. It presents these developments as themes that shaped the decade, though they span different years and contexts.
description_long: A TrumpFile overview dated January 1, 2010 and updated in August 2020 groups four themes across the decade. It connects mall closures with consumer weakness after the financial crisis, describes Fox News as a major information source in the Midwest, and notes that Missouri voters chose presidential candidates who lost nationally in both 2008 and 2012. It also claims that Russian oligarchs invested in U.S. banks, companies, real estate and social-media businesses during the decade after the crash. The overview treats these subjects as part of a broader change in American economic and political life. Missouri’s voting pattern is a discrete historical fact within that account; the other claims refer to separate trends and would need their own dated examples to form individual event entries.

corrected_wording.proposed: TrumpFile publishes a broad overview of 2010s economic and political trends
corrected_wording.reason: The linked page is a decade-wide overview rather than a discrete event, so the title identifies it as a broad trends article instead of a dated Trump action.

source_access_notes: Read the full overview page, which is dated January 1, 2010 and notes an August 1, 2020 update. It contains separate claims about four topics and supplies no underlying sources for them.
blockers: The page is a decade-wide compilation, not a discrete event; it supplies no dated examples or citations for mall closures, Fox News audience claims or Russian investment, and does not document a direct Trump connection.
rationale: The linked page presents a retrospective collage of separate economic and political themes rather than one event; attributing its claims does not provide enough evidence for a useful event narrative.

title: Manhattan DA opens 2010 investigation into Trump SoHo sales claims
description_medium: In 2010, Manhattan prosecutors opened an investigation into whether Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr. had misled buyers about unit sales at Trump SoHo. Prosecutors considered whether the sales statements could support fraud charges. The investigation was dropped in August 2012 after Manhattan District Attorney Cyrus Vance overruled his prosecutors.
description_long: The Manhattan District Attorney’s Major Economic Crimes Bureau opened an investigation in 2010 into Trump SoHo sales representations by Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr. Prosecutors examined claims about how many condominium-hotel units had been sold. By March 2010, a Trump partner’s sworn affidavit reportedly put sales at 15.8 percent, below public figures the Trump children had cited. In August 2010, buyers sued the developers, alleging deceptive sales practices. Prosecutors considered charges under New York law, while the siblings’ lawyers argued that the statements were exaggerated marketing rather than crimes. In 2012, Marc Kasowitz, Donald Trump’s longtime lawyer, met with District Attorney Cyrus Vance after donating $25,000 to Vance’s campaign. Vance returned the donation before the meeting, then overruled prosecutors and dropped the investigation on August 3, 2012. Vance said he did not believe a crime could be proved beyond a reasonable doubt.

corrected_wording.proposed: Manhattan DA opens 2010 investigation into Trump SoHo sales claims
corrected_wording.reason: The 2017 investigation reconstructs the opening and closing of the case and attributes the fraud theory to prosecutors; it contradicts the timeline’s unsupported bribery assertion.

source_access_notes: Read the joint ProPublica/New Yorker investigation, which describes the 2010 opening, prosecutors’ evidence and the 2012 decision to drop the case. The reporting does not support the timeline’s bribery allegation.
blockers: The source dates the investigation opening only to 2010, not March 1; it reports campaign contributions and a prosecutor’s decision but does not establish bribery.
rationale: The 2017 investigation reconstructs the opening and closing of the case and attributes the fraud theory to prosecutors; it contradicts the timeline’s unsupported bribery assertion.

title: Brennan Center warns Project 2025 could pressure platforms over election content
description_medium: The Brennan Center’s analysis of Project 2025 says the plan would pressure social-media companies over election-related content, including through FCC action on content moderation and Section 230. It also warns of proposed retaliation against researchers and election officials. It also discusses federal election-security agencies and researchers who address election falsehoods.
description_long: The Brennan Center analyzed Project 2025 proposals affecting how social-media platforms handle election falsehoods. The plan calls for the Federal Communications Commission to use antidiscrimination rules against platforms that limit political content and to narrow Section 230 protections for user-generated material. The center argued that these measures could deter companies from moderating election misinformation through threatened enforcement and lawsuits. The report also describes proposals to target researchers, government officials and civil-society groups working on election misinformation, and to limit the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s related work. The proposals concern platform content moderation and federal election-security work.

corrected_wording.proposed: Brennan Center warns Project 2025 could pressure platforms over election content
corrected_wording.reason: The cited analysis concerns platform regulation and efforts to counter election falsehoods; it does not support the original claim of mass individual surveillance or algorithmic prosecution.

source_access_notes: Read the Brennan Center analysis of Project 2025’s recommendations concerning platform content moderation, Section 230, researchers and federal election-security agencies.
blockers: The Brennan Center describes proposed legal and agency pressure on platforms and researchers; it does not document implemented individual-user surveillance or algorithmic prosecution.
rationale: The cited analysis concerns platform regulation and efforts to counter election falsehoods; it does not support the original claim of mass individual surveillance or algorithmic prosecution.

title: Robert Mueller outlines FBI focus on Eurasian organized crime and Mogilevich group
description_medium: On January 27, 2011, FBI Director Robert Mueller told New York’s Citizens Crime Commission that transnational criminal networks posed a significant national-security threat. He described FBI Threat Focus Cells established to target Eurasian organized crime, including the Semion Mogilevich Organization, and noted Mogilevich was on the FBI Ten Most Wanted list.
description_long: FBI Director Robert Mueller addressed New York’s Citizens Crime Commission on January 27, 2011, in a speech about the changing threat from organized crime. He described criminal networks operating across legitimate businesses and illicit markets, including human trafficking, health-care fraud and cyber intrusions. Mueller said the FBI had established two Threat Focus Cells the previous year to target Eurasian organized crime. One focused on the Semion Mogilevich Organization; the other focused on the Brother’s Circle. The cells drew personnel from the FBI’s criminal, cyber, counterintelligence and international operations divisions and worked with U.S. and foreign law-enforcement and intelligence partners. Mueller noted that Mogilevich was on the FBI Ten Most Wanted list.

corrected_wording.proposed: Robert Mueller outlines FBI focus on Eurasian organized crime and Mogilevich group
corrected_wording.reason: The FBI transcript supports the speech’s organized-crime assessment and the Mogilevich unit, while disproving the title’s superlative and providing no Trump connection.

source_access_notes: Read Mueller’s complete January 27, 2011 speech in the FBI archive. It identifies the Threat Focus Cells, their targets and the Mogilevich Ten Most Wanted status.
blockers: The FBI speech does not make the “biggest threat to U.S. democracy” statement in the original title, and the record provides no evidence connecting this 2011 speech to Donald Trump.
rationale: The FBI transcript supports the speech’s organized-crime assessment and the Mogilevich unit, while disproving the title’s superlative and providing no Trump connection.
